  PART 1 — QUICK BOOK NOTES
1.1  Syntax Directed Definitions (SDD)
Definition — SDD: a context-free grammar where every grammar symbol is given a set of attributes, and every 
production is given a set of semantic rules that compute those attributes.
Example — SDD for E → E1 + T
Production: E → E1 + T
Semantic Rule: E.val = E1.val + T.val
Meaning: the value of the bigger expression is the sum of its two parts — exactly how a calculator evaluates 3 + 4.
1.2  Syntax Trees
Definition — Syntax Tree: a tree that shows the grammatical structure of a source string, with each interior node 
representing an operation and each leaf a variable or constant.
Example — Syntax tree for a + b * c
        +
       / \
      a   *
         / \
        b   c
The tree shows * binds tighter than +, matching normal maths rules.
1.3  S-Attributed and L-Attributed Definitions
Definition — S-Attributed Definition: an SDD that uses only synthesized attributes — values computed from 
children and passed upward. Works naturally with bottom-up (LR) parsing.
Definition — L-Attributed Definition: an SDD that allows both synthesized attributes and inherited attributes that 
depend only on parent/left-sibling values. Works with top-down parsing.
Example — Everyday analogy
S-attributed is like adding up your monthly expenses from receipts — information flows only upward (child to 
parent).
L-attributed is like a teacher passing today's date down to every student in a row, left to right — information 
flows downward and sideways too.
1.4  Type Systems
Definition — Type System: the set of rules a compiler uses to assign a type to every expression and to check that 
operations are used with compatible types.
Example — Simple type rule

It explains type systems and the role of attributes in semantic analysis. Illustrations include arithmetic expression trees and attribute rules.

1.5  Type Checking
Definition — Type Checking: the process of verifying that the type of an operand matches what an operator 
expects, reporting a type error otherwise.
Example — Type error caught at compile time
int x = "hello";   →   compiler reports: cannot assign a string literal to an int variable.
1.6  Type Equivalence
Definition — Type Equivalence: the rule that decides when two type expressions are considered the same — 
commonly by name (name equivalence) or by structure (structural equivalence).
Example — Name vs structural equivalence
typedef struct {int x; int y;} Point;   struct {int x; int y;} p2;
Under name equivalence, Point and the anonymous struct are different types even though their layout is 
identical.
1.7  Type Conversions
Definition — Type Conversion (Coercion): an automatic or explicit change of a value from one type to another, 
done so an operator or assignment can proceed correctly.
Example — Implicit widening
int i = 5; float f = i;   →   compiler inserts an implicit int-to-float conversion, since this never loses information.
1.8  Intermediate Languages
Definition — Intermediate Representation (IR): a machine-independent form between the source program and 
target code — common forms are syntax trees, DAGs, postfix notation, and three address code.
Example — Postfix vs infix
Infix:  a + b * c     Postfix:  a b c * +
Postfix removes the need for parentheses and precedence rules during code generation.
1.9  Three Address Code (TAC)
Definition — Three Address Code: an intermediate code where every statement has at most one operator on the 
right side and at most three addresses (two operands, one result).
Expression: a = b * c + d * e
TAC:
  t1 = b * c
  t2 = d * e

1.10  Types and Declarations
Definition — Declaration Processing: the compiler phase that records each variable's type and computes its 
storage width and offset in the symbol table as declarations are read.
Example — Offset computation
int a; float b; char c;   →   a at offset 0 (width 4), b at offset 4 (width 4), c at offset 8 (width 1).
1.11  Translation of Expressions
Definition — Expression Translation: the systematic generation of three address code for an expression by 
translating each subtree of its syntax tree and combining the results.
Example — Translating a + b * c
t1 = b * c
t2 = a + t1
The multiplication is translated first because * has higher precedence and appears deeper in the syntax tree.
1.12  Back Patching
Definition — Back Patching: a technique for generating code for boolean expressions and control statements in a 
single pass by leaving the target of a jump instruction incomplete and filling it in later once the target address is 
known.
Example — Why it's needed
For if (a < b) goto L, the compiler often doesn't know the actual instruction number for L yet — so it leaves a blank 
and patches it in once that label's address is fixed.
summary: Declaration processing records variable types, storage width, and offsets in the symbol table. Expression translation generates TAC by traversing syntax trees, respecting operator precedence. Back patching is explained as a single-pass technique for handling incomplete jump targets in boolean and control flow code.

2.1  Syntax Directed Definitions (SDD)
A Syntax Directed Definition attaches attributes to grammar symbols and semantic rules to productions. Every 
time a production is used during parsing, its semantic rule tells the compiler how to compute some value — like 
the numeric result of an expression, the type of a variable, or the generated code.
Attributes are of two kinds:
• Synthesized attribute — computed from the attribute values of the children of a node (flows bottom-up).
• Inherited attribute — computed from the attribute values of the parent and/or siblings (flows top-down or 
left-to-right).
Production Semantic Rule Meaning
E → E1 + T E.val = E1.val + T.val add the two sub-values
E → T E.val = T.val copy value upward
T → T1 * F T.val = T1.val * F.val multiply the two sub-values
F → ( E ) F.val = E.val value of parenthesised expr
F → id F.val = id.lexval look up the identifier's value
Example — Real-time example — a billing calculator
Think of a shop billing app evaluating quantity * price + tax. Each time the app combines two numbers, it is 
silently applying a semantic rule identical to E.val = E1.val + T.val.
This is exactly the mechanism compilers use to evaluate constant expressions during compilation (constant 
folding).
2.2  Syntax Trees and DAGs
A syntax tree represents the essential structure of a program in a more compact form than a parse tree — 
operators become interior nodes and operands become leaves, with no nodes for chain productions like E → T 
→ F.
A Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) goes one step further: if the same sub-expression appears more than once, the 
DAG reuses a single node instead of duplicating it, exposing common sub-expressions.
Example — Syntax tree vs DAG for a + a * (b - c) + (b - c) * d
The sub-expression (b - c) appears twice.
A syntax tree draws two separate (b - c) subtrees.
A DAG draws (b - c) only once and lets both '*' operations point to that single node — this is the theoretical basis 
for common sub-expression elimination, a real optimisation used in GCC and every industrial compiler.
2.3  S-Attributed and L-Attributed Definitions
summary: Syntax Directed Definitions attach attributes to grammar symbols and semantic rules to productions, distinguishing synthesized (bottom‑up) and inherited (top‑down) attributes. The notes illustrate semantic rules for arithmetic expressions and explain how syntax trees and DAGs represent program structure, with DAGs enabling common sub‑expression elimination. S‑Attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes, while L‑Attributed definitions allow inherited attributes that depend only on left or parent symbols.

S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes. Because values only ever flow upward from children to 
parent, they can be evaluated naturally during a bottom-up (LR) parse, simply by computing each attribute when 
its production is reduced.
L-attributed definitions allow inherited attributes too, but only in a restricted, left-to-right way: an inherited 
attribute of a symbol on the right side of a production may depend only on attributes of the production's left 
side, or on attributes of symbols to its left. This restriction is exactly what makes L-attributed definitions safe to 
evaluate during a single left-to-right depth-first parse (used in top-down / recursive-descent parsing).
How to identify which kind an SDD is
Look at every semantic rule for inherited attributes referencing anything to the right — if none exist, and only 
children feed the parent, it's S-attributed.
If inherited attributes exist but only ever look left or up, it's L-attributed. If an inherited attribute needs a value 
from the right, it is neither, and needs multiple parsing passes or attribute grammars with global rules.
Example — Real-time example — a form validator
A web form that passes today's date down into every 'age' field (inherited, parent → children) and then collects 
validation results back up to show one summary error box (synthesized, children → parent) is behaving like an L-
attributed definition.
2.4  Type Systems
A type system is a set of rules that assigns a type to every expression in a program and defines which operations 
are legal between which types. Its two jobs are: preventing meaningless operations (like adding a string to a 
boolean) and enabling the compiler to choose the correct machine instructions and storage layout for each 
value.
Type systems are classified as:
• Static typing — types are checked at compile time (C, Java, our CS4501 running examples).
• Dynamic typing — types are checked at run time (Python, JavaScript).
• Strong typing — no silent, unsafe conversions are allowed; Weak typing — many implicit conversions are 
allowed.
Example — Real-time example
When you write int total = quantity * price; in C, the compiler's type system decides at compile time that quantity 
and price (both int) multiply to give an int — no runtime check is needed, which is why compiled C code runs 
faster than an equivalent Python script.
2.5  Type Checking
A type checker verifies that the type of each operand matches what the corresponding operator expects, using 
type rules built into the compiler's semantic analysis phase. It works over the same syntax-directed framework 
as Section 2.1 — every expression gets a 'type' attribute in addition to its 'val' attribute.
Rule Pattern Type Rule
E → E1 + E2 if E1.type = E2.type = int then E.type = int; if either is float 
then E.type = float
E → E1 and E2 if E1.type = E2.type = bool then E.type = bool, else type-
error
summary: S‑Attributed definitions compute attributes during a bottom‑up parse, whereas L‑Attributed definitions permit inherited attributes that depend only on left or parent symbols, enabling single left‑to‑right depth‑first evaluation. The material covers type systems (static vs dynamic, strong vs weak), type checking rules, type equivalence (name vs structural), and type conversions (implicit vs explicit). It also introduces intermediate representations, especially Three‑Address Code, symbol table handling of types, offsets, and the translation of expressions into TAC, culminating in back‑patching for control‑flow.

2.6  Type Equivalence
Two types are equivalent if the compiler treats them as interchangeable. There are two common definitions:
• Name equivalence — two types are the same only if they share the same declared name.
• Structural equivalence — two types are the same if they have the same structure (same fields, in the same 
order, with the same types), regardless of name.
Example — Real-time example
typedef int Meters; typedef int Feet;
Under name equivalence, a Meters value cannot be assigned directly to a Feet variable even though both are 
really int — this is exactly how languages like Ada prevent unit-mixing bugs (e.g. the 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter 
loss, caused by mixing metric and imperial units).
2.7  Type Conversions (Coercion)
When an operator or assignment involves mismatched types, the compiler inserts a conversion. Conversions are 
either:
• Implicit (coercion) — inserted automatically by the compiler, usually only in the 'widening' direction (int → 
float) so no data is lost.
• Explicit (casting) — written by the programmer, e.g. (int) 3.99, which may lose information (narrowing).
Expression Compiler Action Result
int i = 5; float f = i; implicit widening int→float f = 5.0
float g = 5.9; int k = (int) g; explicit narrowing float→int k = 5 (fraction truncated)
Example — Real-time example — currency calculation bug
float total = 19.99 * 3;  printed as 59.97000123 due to floating point widening — a real reason financial software 
uses fixed-point/decimal types instead of float, to avoid conversion precision loss.
2.8  Intermediate Languages
An intermediate representation (IR) sits between the source program and the target machine code. It lets a 
compiler support many source languages and many target machines without writing a separate front end/back 
end for every combination (this is exactly the design GCC and LLVM use).
Common intermediate forms:
Form Description
Postfix Notation operators follow operands; no parentheses needed, e.g. a 
b c * +
Syntax Tree / DAG tree/graph structure showing the grammatical structure
summary: Type checking assigns a type to each identifier by looking up the symbol table, and the example shows how a strong‑typed compiler flags the misuse of assignment in a conditional (e.g., `if (marks = 90)`), catching a common beginner error before runtime.

Example — Real-time example
LLVM IR is exactly this idea in industrial practice — Clang (C/C++), Rust, and Swift all compile down to the same 
LLVM IR, which is then optimised once and translated to x86, ARM, or any other target — saving enormous 
engineering effort.
2.9  Three Address Code (TAC)
Three Address Code is the most widely used intermediate representation. Every TAC statement has the general 
form x = y op z, where op is a single operator and there are at most three addresses (two operands and a result). 
Complex expressions are broken into a sequence of such statements using compiler-generated temporary 
variables (t1, t2, ...).
Common TAC statement types:
Statement Type Example
Assignment x = y op z
Copy x = y
Unconditional jump goto L
Conditional jump if x relop y goto L
Procedure call param x  /  call p, n
Indexed / pointer x = y[i]   or   *p = x
TAC is typically implemented internally as quadruples (op, arg1, arg2, result) or triples (op, arg1, arg2, referring 
to statement position instead of a named result).
Example — Quadruple table for a = b * c + d * c
( * , b, c, t1 )
( * , d, c, t2 )
( + , t1, t2, t3 )
( = , t3, - , a )
2.10  Types and Declarations
When the compiler processes a declaration, it must record in the symbol table: the variable's type, its width 
(bytes needed), and its offset (position relative to the start of its storage area, such as an activation record). This 
groundwork is essential before any code generation can happen, because every later TAC instruction that reads 
or writes a variable needs to know exactly where it lives.
A running 'offset' counter is maintained as declarations are processed left to right; each new variable is placed at 
the current offset, and the offset is then advanced by that variable's width.
Example — Worked declaration block
int a; char b; float c; int d;
widths: int=4, char=1, float=4
a: offset 0   b: offset 4   c: offset 5   d: offset 9
summary: Three‑Address Code (TAC) is a widely used IR where each statement has the form `x = y op z`; LLVM IR exemplifies this approach. TAC is often represented as quadruples or triples, and the notes provide examples of TAC generation for arithmetic expressions. The section also explains how the compiler records variable types, widths, and offsets in the symbol table to support code generation.

2.11  Translation of Expressions
Expression translation combines syntax-directed definitions (2.1) with three address code (2.9): each non-
terminal gets a synthesized attribute 'code' (the TAC generated so far) and 'addr' (the address/temporary 
holding its value). The rules build code bottom-up, generating a new temporary at every operator node.
Production Semantic Action
E → E1 + E2 E.addr = newtemp(); emit(E.addr = E1.addr + E2.addr)
E → E1 * E2 E.addr = newtemp(); emit(E.addr = E1.addr * E2.addr)
E → ( E1 ) E.addr = E1.addr
E → id E.addr = id (lookup symbol table entry)
Example — Full worked translation of a + b * c
Step 1 (F → id, T → F): b.addr = b, c.addr = c
Step 2 (T → T * F): t1 = b * c
Step 3 (F → id, T → F): a.addr = a
Step 4 (E → E + T): t2 = a + t1
Final TAC:  t1 = b * c   ;   t2 = a + t1
2.12  Back Patching
For boolean expressions and control-flow statements (if, while, for), the target label of a jump instruction is 
often not known at the moment the jump instruction itself is generated — the label might belong to code that 
appears later. Back patching solves this in a single compiler pass:
• Generate the jump instruction, but leave its target field blank.
• Add the instruction's own position to a list associated with the appropriate attribute (truelist, falselist, or 
nextlist).
• Once the real target address becomes known (e.g. we reach the code for the 'then' branch), patch every 
instruction in the list with that address.
Two key functions used throughout: makelist(i) creates a new list containing only instruction i; merge(p1, p2) 
concatenates two lists; backpatch(list, addr) fills in addr as the target for every instruction in list.
Example — Backpatching if (a < b) then S
100: if a < b goto _   (target unknown → added to E.truelist)
101: goto _            (target unknown → added to E.falselist)
102: <code for S begins here>
Once we reach 102, we call backpatch(E.truelist, 102) — instruction 100 is patched to 'goto 102'.
Instruction 101 remains in falselist, to be patched once we know where control goes if the condition is false (e.g. 
after the whole if-statement, or an else branch).
Why this matters in real compilers
Back patching is exactly how a single-pass compiler (like early C compilers) generates working jump targets for 
nested if/while/for statements without a second pass over the code — it's the practical trick that makes one-pass

2.13  Syntax Directed Translation (SDT) Schemes and Predictive Translators
An SDD specifies WHAT a translation computes, but deliberately leaves open WHEN each semantic rule fires 
during parsing. A Syntax Directed Translation (SDT) scheme is the implementation-ready counterpart: it embeds 
semantic actions directly inside the production body at the exact point they should execute, fixing the 
evaluation order. This is the notation actually used to build a working translator.
Definition — Predictive Translator: a top-down, table-driven translator that selects the correct production for a 
non-terminal using only that non-terminal and one token of lookahead (no backtracking), firing embedded 
semantic actions as it goes so the translation is produced as a side effect of parsing.
Because a predictive parser commits to a production the moment it sees the lookahead token, its actions must 
fire in a strictly pinned-down order -- which is precisely what an SDT (not a plain SDD) provides. Building one 
requires an LL(1) parsing table, constructed in five steps:
• Step 1: Eliminate left recursion (A -> Aa | b becomes A -> bA', A' -> aA' | eps) and left-factor productions 
sharing a common prefix.
• Step 2: Compute FIRST for every non-terminal, then FOLLOW for every non-terminal (starting with $ in 
FOLLOW of the start symbol).
• Step 3: Build table M[A,a]: place A->alpha in M[A,a] for every a in FIRST(alpha); if eps is in FIRST(alpha), also 
place it in M[A,b] for every b in FOLLOW(A).
• Step 4: To parse, trace a stack starting with $ and the start symbol: pop a non-terminal and push 
M[top,token]'s right side (reversed); pop and match a terminal directly against the input. Stop when both 
stack and input show only $.
• Step 5 (error handling): a blank table cell signals a syntax error; if the current token is in FOLLOW(A), panic-
mode recovery simply pops A and continues, treating it as if A had matched empty input.
FIRST and FOLLOW rules (memorise these)
FIRST(X): if X is a terminal, FIRST(X)={X}. If X->eps, add eps. If X->Y1Y2...Yk, add FIRST(Y1)-{eps}, and continue 
adding FIRST(Yi) for each further Yi only while every earlier Yj can derive eps; add eps itself only if ALL Yi can 
derive eps.
FOLLOW(A): $ is in FOLLOW(start symbol). For A->aBb, add FIRST(b)-{eps} to FOLLOW(B). For A->aB, or if eps is in 
FIRST(b), add all of FOLLOW(A) to FOLLOW(B) as well.
Example — Worked LL(1) table and trace for E->TE'|.., translating id+id*id
Table (rows E,E',T,T',F; columns id,+,*,(,),$) is built from FIRST/FOLLOW exactly as in Section 2.13 Step 3.
Tracing the stack against id+id*id produces the parse E->TE', T->FT', F->id, T'->eps, E'->+TE', T->FT', F->id, T'->*FT', 
F->id, T'->eps, E'->eps.
If a print action fires right after each token is matched or each production completes, the emitted order is id id id 
* + -- the correct postfix form, confirming precedence is respected purely by parse order.
2.14  Dependency Graphs and Attribute Evaluation Order
Once an SDD mixes synthesized and inherited attributes freely, it is no longer obvious that a simple bottom-up 
or top-down pass will compute every attribute before it is needed. A dependency graph makes this explicit: for 
every attribute instance at every parse-tree node, draw an edge M -> N whenever attribute N's semantic rule 
reads attribute M's value. A valid evaluation order is then any topological sort of this graph -- an order in which 
every node appears after all the nodes with edges pointing into it.
summary: This page explains Syntax Directed Translation (SDT) schemes and predictive translators, detailing how semantic actions are embedded in productions for LL(1) parsing. It outlines the five‑step construction of an LL(1) parsing table, including FIRST/FOLLOW computation and error handling. It also introduces dependency graphs for attribute evaluation order, showing how to topologically sort attributes.

Definition — Annotated Parse Tree: a parse tree in which every node is labelled with the value of its attribute(s), 
typically shown once evaluation is complete.
For a purely S-attributed SDD, every edge in the dependency graph points from child to parent, so a plain post-
order traversal is always already a valid topological order -- this is exactly why S-attributed definitions need no 
separate dependency-graph analysis in practice: bottom-up parsing already visits nodes in a compatible order.
Example — Dependency graph and evaluation order for postfix ab+c*de-/
Decoding the postfix string with a stack gives the tree for ((a+b)*c)/(d-e).
Naming internal nodes N1=a+b, N2=N1*c, N3=d-e, N4(root)=N2/N3, the dependency graph has edges a->N1, b-
>N1, N1->N2, c->N2, d->N3, e->N3, N2->N4, N3->N4.
A topological sort simply evaluates every leaf first, then any node whose children are already done, repeating up 
to the root: a,b (leaves) -> N1 -> c (leaf) -> N2 -> d,e (leaves) -> N3 -> N4 (root).
How to solve a notation-conversion problem step by step
Step 1 (decoding postfix): scan left to right with a stack; push operands; on an operator, pop the required 
operands and push the combined sub-expression back -- the last item left is the tree's root.
Step 2: draw the syntax tree from the fully-reduced expression.
Step 3: for infix, traverse IN-ORDER (adding parentheses per operator); for prefix, traverse PRE-ORDER; for 
postfix, traverse POST-ORDER of the same tree -- all three notations are just different traversals of one tree, 
never three different trees.
2.15  Type Expressions, Static vs Dynamic Checking
Section 2.4 introduced type systems informally; this section adds the formal notation compilers use internally to 
represent a type, plus the distinction between when a type is actually checked.
Definition — Type Expression: a formal notation for a type, built either from a basic type (integer, real, char, 
boolean, void) or by applying a type constructor -- array(n,T), pointer(T), T1 x T2 (product/record), or T1 -> T2 
(function) -- to smaller type expressions.
Checking Style When It Happens Trade-off
Static typing Compile time, before the program 
runs
Catches errors early, no runtime cost, 
but less flexible
Dynamic typing Run time, as each operation executes More flexible (e.g. duck typing), but 
adds runtime overhead and errors 
surface later
How to solve a type-checking problem step by step
Step 1: draw (or imagine) the expression tree; note the declared type of every leaf (variable/literal).
Step 2: work bottom-up -- at every operator node, look up both children's already-computed types.
Step 3: apply the type rule table to decide this node's result type, inserting a conversion instruction into the TAC 
if a type had to be widened.
Step 4: if no rule matches, assign type_error to this node and let it propagate upward as the node's type -- do not 
keep re-deriving further mismatches from an already-errored subtree.
Step 5: the type at the ROOT is the type of the whole expression.

P.1  Problem 1 — Construct an SDD and evaluate it for 3 * 4 + 5
Step 1 — Identify the grammar and attribute. We use E→E+T | T, T→T*F | F, F→(E) | digit, with one synthesized 
attribute val on every non-terminal, meaning 'the numeric value this subtree represents.'
Step 2 — Parse the input bottom-up. Because * has higher precedence than +, the grammar's structure forces 3 
* 4 to be reduced first (it becomes a single T), and only afterwards is + applied at the E level. This is precisely 
why this grammar family (with separate E and T levels) enforces correct precedence without needing explicit 
precedence rules.
Step 3 — Apply the semantic rule at every reduction, in the exact order the parser reduces:
Parse: (3 * 4) + 5
F -> 3        F.val = 3
F -> 4        F.val = 4
T -> T * F    T.val = 3 * 4 = 12
F -> 5        F.val = 5
T -> F        T.val = 5
E -> E + T    E.val = 12 + 5 = 17
Final Answer: E.val = 17
Step 4 — Interpret the result. Notice that val is synthesized purely bottom-up: each rule only reads the val of its 
own children, never anything from outside the subtree. This is exactly the S-attributed pattern from Section 1.3 / 
2.3, which is why this SDD can be evaluated directly during an LR parse with no extra passes.
Common mistake to avoid
Students often apply E -> E + T before T -> T * F is fully reduced. Always finish reducing the higher-precedence 
subtree (T, from *) completely before combining it at the E level -- this mirrors the actual bottom-up parse order, 
not the left-to-right reading order of the expression.
P.2  Problem 2 — Draw the syntax tree and DAG for (a + b) * (a + b) + c
Step 1 — Build the plain syntax tree first. Every operator becomes an interior node; a syntax tree makes no 
attempt to detect repetition, so (a + b) is drawn twice, as two completely separate subtrees, even though they 
are structurally identical.
Step 2 — Convert to a DAG by scanning for repeated subtrees. Two subtrees are 'the same' in a DAG if they have 
the same operator and the same operand nodes. Here, both '+' nodes have operands a and b -- so they collapse 
into a single shared node.
DAG (shared sub-expression):
        +
       / \
      *   c
     / \
    +   +   <- these two '+' nodes for (a+b) COLLAPSE into ONE node in the DAG
   /\   /\
  a  b a  b
DAG version: only ONE '+' node for (a+b), reused by both operands of '*'.
Step 3 — Explain the benefit. If this were compiled as a syntax tree, the compiler would generate code to 
compute a + b twice. As a DAG, it computes a + b once, stores it in a temporary, and reuses that temporary for

translator does not automatically detect repetition -- that optimisation belongs to the DAG step from Problem 2, 
not to basic TAC generation):

rearrange during optimisation but take more memory. Triples save memory by referring to earlier statements by 
their position number instead of a temporary name, but this makes rearranging code during optimisation 
harder, since moving a triple changes every position number that refers to it.

P.8  Problem 8 — Translate while (a < b) do a = a + 1 using backpatching
Step 1 — Unlike if, a while loop must return to re-test its condition after every iteration, so the very first step is 
to save the instruction number where the condition test begins -- call it the begin label.
Step 2 — Generate the conditional jump for the test (truelist) and the jump for loop exit (falselist), exactly as in 
Problem 7.
Step 3 — Once we reach the first instruction of the loop body, backpatch truelist to that address.
Step 4 — After the loop body's last instruction, generate an unconditional jump back to the saved begin label -- 
this is what actually forms the loop.
Step 5 — Once we reach the first instruction after the whole while statement, backpatch falselist to that 
address.
100: if a < b goto 102       (begin label = 100, E.truelist={100})
101: goto _                  (E.falselist={101}, will exit loop)
102: t1 = a + 1
103: a = t1
104: goto 100                <- unconditional jump BACK to re-test condition
105: <code after while>      <- backpatch(E.falselist, 105): instr 101 -> 'goto 105'
Why while needs a saved 'begin' label but if doesn't
A while loop must jump back to re-check its condition every iteration, so the compiler must remember the 
instruction number where the condition test starts (100 here) -- this is the one detail students most often forget 
in exams.

P.10  Problem 10 — Translate the boolean expression a < b and c < d using 
backpatching
Step 1 — Recall the short-circuit rule for 'and': if the first operand is false, the whole expression is false 
immediately, and the second operand should not even be evaluated.
Step 2 — Translate the first comparison a < b. If it's true, control must fall through to test the second 
comparison -- so its truelist is not patched yet, it simply continues to the next instruction. If it's false, the whole 
expression is false, so its falselist becomes part of the overall expression's falselist directly.
Step 3 — Translate the second comparison c < d. Its truelist and falselist become the truelist and falselist of the 
entire 'and' expression.
100: if a < b goto 102        (fall through on true -- no jump needed, so control just 
continues)
101: goto _                   (falselist of a<b joins the falselist of the whole 
expression)
102: if c < d goto _          (this becomes the truelist of the whole expression)
103: goto _                   (this joins the falselist of the whole expression)
Overall: truelist = {102}, falselist = {101, 103}
Key idea examiners test here
The defining feature of 'and' translation is that the first operand's TRUE case does NOT jump anywhere -- it just 
falls through into the code for the second operand. Only the FALSE case of the first operand needs an explicit 
jump (to skip evaluating the second operand entirely) -- this is what implements short-circuit evaluation.

  PART 4 — PART A (2 MARK) QUESTION BANK
Q1. What is a Syntax Directed Definition (SDD)?
Ans: An SDD is a context-free grammar in which every grammar symbol carries a set of attributes, and every 
production has an associated semantic rule defining how those attributes are computed. It specifies WHAT a 
translation computes without fixing WHEN each rule fires -- e.g. E->E1+T with rule E.val=E1.val+T.val.
Q2. Differentiate an SDD from a Syntax Directed Translation (SDT) scheme.
Ans: An SDD leaves the evaluation order of its semantic rules unspecified. An SDT embeds semantic actions 
directly inside the production body at the exact point they must execute, fixing that order -- which is what a 
predictive (top-down) translator needs, since it commits to actions as it parses left to right.
Q3. Differentiate synthesized and inherited attributes.
Ans: A synthesized attribute's value at a node is computed from its CHILDREN, so information flows bottom-up 
(e.g. E.val=E1.val+T.val). An inherited attribute's value comes from its PARENT or LEFT SIBLINGS, so information 
flows top-down or left-to-right (e.g. passing a declared type down to every identifier in a list).
Q4. What is an annotated parse tree?
Ans: A parse tree in which every node is labelled with the value of its computed attribute(s) -- for example, 
showing E.val=17 written directly at the E node after evaluating 3*4+5.
Q5. What is a dependency graph, and how is it used?
Ans: A graph with one edge M->N for every attribute instance N whose semantic rule reads attribute M's value. 
A valid evaluation order is any topological sort of this graph; for a purely S-attributed SDD every edge points 
child-to-parent, so post-order traversal alone is already a valid order.
Q6. What is a syntax tree?
Ans: A compact tree representing a program's grammatical structure, with operators/keywords as interior nodes 
and operands as leaves; nodes for symbols with no semantic meaning (like parentheses, or chain productions 
such as E->T->F) are omitted.
Q7. How does a DAG differ from a syntax tree?
Ans: A Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is built the same way as a syntax tree, but before creating a new node it 
checks whether an identical node (same operator, same children) already exists -- if so it reuses that node 
instead of duplicating it, exposing repeated sub-expressions for optimisation.
Q8. Define S-attributed definition.
Ans: An SDD in which every attribute is synthesized. Because values only ever flow upward from children to 
parent, an S-attributed SDD can always be evaluated during a single bottom-up (LR) parse, with no extra passes 
needed.
Q9. Define L-attributed definition.
Ans: An SDD that also allows inherited attributes, but only under the restriction that an inherited attribute may 
depend solely on the parent's attributes or on attributes of symbols strictly to its LEFT in the same production -- 
this restriction is what keeps it evaluable in one left-to-right, depth-first (top-down) pass.
Q10. What is a predictive translator, and what grammar property does it require?

It emphasizes how attribute flow determines evaluation order and the requirements for LL(1) grammars. The page serves as a concise reference for foundational compiler theory.

Q11. State the rule for computing FIRST(X).
Ans: If X is a terminal, FIRST(X)={X}. If X->eps, add eps. If X->Y1Y2...Yk, add FIRST(Y1)-{eps}, and keep adding 
FIRST(Yi) for later Yi only while every earlier Yj can derive eps; add eps itself only if ALL Yi can derive eps.
Q12. State the rule for computing FOLLOW(A).
Ans: $ is in FOLLOW of the start symbol. For A->aBb, add FIRST(b)-{eps} to FOLLOW(B). For A->aB, or whenever 
eps is in FIRST(b), add all of FOLLOW(A) to FOLLOW(B) as well.
Q13. What is a type system?
Ans: The set of rules a compiler uses to assign a type to every expression and to check that each operator's 
operands have compatible types, flagging incompatible combinations as type_error.
Q14. What is a type expression?
Ans: A formal notation for a type, built either from a basic type (integer, real, char, boolean, void) or by applying 
a constructor -- array(n,T), pointer(T), T1xT2 (product/record), or T1->T2 (function) -- to smaller type 
expressions.
Q15. Differentiate static and dynamic type checking.
Ans: Static checking happens at compile time, before the program runs, catching errors early with no runtime 
cost. Dynamic checking happens at run time, as each operation executes -- more flexible, but with runtime 
overhead and later error discovery.
Q16. What is type checking?
Ans: The process of verifying, at every operator node of an expression, that its operands' types match what that 
operator legally expects -- computed bottom-up, reporting type_error otherwise and letting that error 
propagate upward without re-deriving further mismatches.
Q17. Define name equivalence of types.
Ans: Two type expressions are equivalent only if they were declared under the exact same type name, even if 
their underlying structure is identical -- e.g. typedef int Meters; typedef int Feet; makes Meters and Feet distinct 
types.
Q18. Define structural equivalence of types.
Ans: Two type expressions are equivalent if they are built from the same constructors over equivalent 
components, regardless of what they are named -- e.g. pointer(integer) is structurally equivalent to any other 
pointer(integer), whatever each is called.
Q19. What is type coercion?
Ans: An implicit (automatic) conversion of a value from one type to another, inserted by the compiler so an 
operation or assignment can proceed -- almost always in the widening direction (e.g. int to float), since widening 
never loses information.
Q20. Differentiate widening and narrowing conversions.
Ans: Widening converts to a larger/more general type without data loss (int to float) and is usually done 
implicitly. Narrowing converts to a smaller/less general type and may lose information (float to int, truncating 
the fraction), so it is normally written explicitly as a cast.
Q21. What is an intermediate representation (IR)?

Ans: A machine-independent form that sits between the source program and target machine code, making a 
compiler easier to retarget (only the code generator changes) and easier to optimise once, for every target. 
Common forms: postfix notation, syntax trees/DAGs, and three address code.
Q22. Define Three Address Code (TAC).
Ans: An intermediate code form where each instruction has at most ONE operator on the right side, of the form 
x=y op z, using compiler-generated temporaries (t1, t2, ...) to hold intermediate values.
Q23. What is a quadruple?
Ans: A four-field TAC record (op, arg1, arg2, result) that stores one instruction with its result named explicitly, 
e.g. x:=y*z becomes (*, y, z, x).
Q24. What is a triple?
Ans: A three-field TAC record (op, arg1, arg2) with no explicit result field; a later instruction refers to an earlier 
one's result by that statement's position number instead of a temporary name, saving memory at the cost of 
harder reordering during optimisation.
Q25. What is an indirect triple, and why is it useful?
Ans: A triple table plus a separate array of statement pointers giving the execution order. Because optimisation 
passes often reorder or delete instructions, indirect triples let the pointer array be edited alone, leaving the 
triple table itself untouched.
Q26. Why are declarations processed before code generation?
Ans: The compiler must record each variable's type, storage width, and offset in the symbol table first, since 
every later TAC instruction that reads or writes that variable compiles down to a memory access at 
variable_base+offset -- code generation cannot be correct without this groundwork.
Q27. How is an array reference such as a[i] translated into TAC?
Ans: The index is first converted into a byte offset by multiplying it by the element width (t=i*w), and then an 
indexed load/store instruction (a[t] or t2:=a[t]) accesses the actual array element -- every array access costs this 
one extra multiply unless the compiler can prove the offset at compile time.
Q28. What is backpatching?
Ans: A one-pass code-generation technique: jump instructions whose real target is not yet known are emitted 
with a blank target field, and their instruction numbers are recorded in a list; once the true target address 
becomes known, backpatch() fills it into every jump in that list.
Q29. What are truelist and falselist in backpatching?
Ans: Lists of instruction numbers whose jump targets are still unresolved -- truelist holds jumps to take when the 
boolean expression evaluates true, falselist holds jumps to take when it evaluates false.
Q30. Name the three backpatching helper functions.
Ans: makelist(i) creates a new list containing only instruction i; merge(p1,p2) concatenates two lists into one; 
backpatch(list,addr) fills in addr as the target of every instruction recorded in list.

Q1. Construct the syntax tree and show step-by-step attribute evaluation for 
(a+b)*(c-d) using SDD. (13)
Introduction
This question tests whether you can build a syntax tree from an expression and then correctly apply an S-
attributed SDD to evaluate it. Since (a+b)*(c-d) has two independent parenthesised sub-expressions combined 
by multiplication, the tree naturally has two subtrees feeding one root.
Step 1 — Build the Syntax Tree
The root is the '*' operator, since multiplication is applied last (after both additions/subtractions inside the 
parentheses are resolved). Its left child is the '+' subtree for (a+b), and its right child is the '-' subtree for (c-d). 
Each leaf (a, b, c, d) is an identifier node carrying its own value from the symbol table.
        E.val = E1.val * E2.val
       /                       \
  E1:(a+b)                 E2:(c-d)
  val=a.val+b.val          val=c.val-d.val
  /       \                 /       \
id(a)    id(b)            id(c)    id(d)
Step 2 — Apply the SDD Bottom-Up
Since every rule here only reads its own children's values, this SDD is S-attributed, and evaluation proceeds 
strictly bottom-up: first the four leaves (a.val, b.val, c.val, d.val) are fetched from the symbol table; next E1.val = 
a.val + b.val and E2.val = c.val - d.val are computed independently (their order relative to each other does not 
matter, since neither depends on the other); finally the root combines them: E.val = E1.val * E2.val.
Conclusion
Because no attribute here ever needs information from a parent or a sibling, one single post-order traversal of 
the tree is guaranteed sufficient to compute every value correctly -- this is exactly the defining property of an S-
attributed definition, and it is why such SDDs map naturally onto bottom-up (LR) parsing, where a production's 
semantic rule can simply fire the moment that production is reduced.

Every edge in this graph points from a child toward its parent, with no edge ever pointing backward or sideways

Q3. Design a predictive translator for arithmetic expressions. Generate translation 
for id+id*id. Show parsing table and step-by-step translation. (13)
Introduction
A predictive translator needs an LL(1) parsing table built from FIRST and FOLLOW sets, plus semantic actions 
embedded in each production (an SDT, not a bare SDD) so that the translation -- here, converting infix to postfix

recursive productions at all.

E' - E'->+TE' - - E'->eps E'->eps

Q4. Generate three-address code for a = (b+c)*(d-e)/f. Show syntax tree, TAC with 
temporaries, and optimized TAC. (13)
Introduction
This expression has three operators (+, -, *, /) combined across two levels of precedence, so its translation 
exercises the full bottom-up TAC generation scheme: children's temporaries must be computed before each 
parent operator's instruction can be emitted.
Step 1 — Draw the Syntax Tree
The outermost operator is '/', dividing the product (b+c)*(d-e) by f. Its left child is '*', whose own children are 
the '+' subtree (b+c) and the '-' subtree (d-e).
Step 2 — Generate TAC Bottom-Up
t1 := b + c
t2 := d - e
t3 := t1 * t2
t4 := t3 / f
a  := t4
Step 3 — Check for Optimisation Opportunities
No sub-expression here repeats -- b+c and d-e are computed exactly once each and used exactly once -- so this 
code is already minimal at 4 operator instructions. The only further optimisation available at this stage is 
temporary/register reuse once a value is no longer live (a Unit V concern, not something TAC generation itself 
changes).
Conclusion
This example demonstrates the general rule: the number of TAC instructions generated for an expression equals 
exactly the number of operators in it, provided no common sub-expression is repeated -- confirming the 
translation is both correct and already optimal at the intermediate-code level.

Q6. Explain type systems with examples. Design a simple type checker for arithmetic 
expressions with integer and float types. (13)
Introduction
A type system's job is twofold: assign a type to every expression in the program, and enforce that every operator 
only ever receives operand types it is defined for -- a type checker is simply the algorithm that carries this out, 
expressed as an SDD with an added 'type' attribute alongside any value attribute.
Step 1 — State the Type Rule for Arithmetic Operators
For +, -, *, /: int op int gives int (no conversion). float op float gives float (no conversion). int op float, in either 
order, requires widening the int operand to float first (via an inttoreal conversion), and the result is float. Any 
other combination is a type_error.
Step 2 — Apply the Rule Bottom-Up to a + b * c (a:int, b:int, c:float)
Precedence dictates b*c is checked first: b is int, c is float, so this is the mixed case -- b is widened, and the result 
type is float. Next, a+(b*c) is checked: a is int, the previous result is float -- again the mixed case, so a is widened, 
and the overall expression type is float.
Conclusion
A type checker built this way is simply a recursive, bottom-up walk of the expression tree, applying exactly this 
one rule table at every operator node -- it needs no special-casing for deeper expressions, since each operator 
node only ever needs the types its own two children have already computed.

Introduction
Before a compiler can decide whether one type may be used where another is expected, it must first decide 
what 'the same type' even means -- this is the role of a type equivalence rule, and languages differ in which one 
they adopt.
Step 1 — Define Structural Equivalence
Two type expressions are structurally equivalent if they are built from the same constructors applied to 
equivalent components, regardless of what either type was named. For example, pointer(integer) is structurally 
equivalent to any other pointer(integer), no matter what each was called in source code.
Step 2 — Define Name Equivalence
Two type expressions are name-equivalent only if they were declared under the exact same type name. Even if 
type A=int; type B=int; produces two types with identical structure, A and B are NOT equivalent under this 
stricter rule -- this catches unit-mixing mistakes that structural equivalence alone would silently allow.
Step 3 — Describe How a Checker Applies Each Rule
A structural-equivalence checker recursively compares constructor and components (e.g. for two array types, 
both the element type AND the declared size must match). A name-equivalence checker compares only the 
declared type identifiers directly, without recursing into structure at all -- it is a simple lookup, not a recursive 
comparison.
Conclusion
Most languages pick one rule consistently for user-defined types: structural equivalence gives more flexibility 
(any two types 'shaped' the same interoperate), while name equivalence gives more safety (distinct concepts 
stay distinct even if their underlying representation happens to coincide).
Q8. Demonstrate type conversions by generating intermediate code for float a; int b; 
a = b + 3.5; Show conversion steps. (13)
Introduction
This statement mixes an int variable, a float literal, and a float target, so it exercises the compiler's implicit 
widening rule at two different points: once inside the addition, and once (trivially) at the final assignment.
Step 1 — Type-Check the Right-Hand Side
b is declared int; the literal 3.5 is float. Since these differ, the widening rule applies: b must be converted to float 
before the addition can proceed. The compiler inserts this conversion automatically -- the programmer never 
writes it.
Step 2 — Generate the TAC with the Conversion Made Explicit
t1 := inttoreal(b)     // widen b: int -> float
t2 := t1 + 3.5         // float addition
a  := t2               // a is float -- direct copy, no further conversion needed
Conclusion
Because a is already declared float and t2 is float (the result of the addition), the final assignment needs no 
conversion of its own -- only the mismatched operand inside the addition ever needed widening. This 
demonstrates that type conversion is applied locally, at exactly the operator or assignment where a mismatch is 
detected, not globally across the whole statement.

Group B (Q10-Q17) — Boolean Expressions, Backpatching & SDT Notations
Q10. Translate the boolean expression (a<b) and (c>d) into three-address code. 
Show short-circuit evaluation with labels. (13)
Introduction
Short-circuit evaluation of 'and' means the second operand is only evaluated if the first is already true -- this 
question asks for that behaviour to be made explicit in labelled TAC, rather than left implicit in a backpatched 
skeleton.
Step 1 — Translate the First Operand a<b
If a<b is true, execution must continue to test c>d; if false, the whole expression is immediately false and c>d 
must never be evaluated.
Step 2 — Translate the Second Operand and the Result-Setting Code
100: if a < b goto 102        104: t := 1     // TRUE
101: goto 106                 105: goto 107
102: if c > d goto 104        106: t := 0     // FALSE
103: goto 106                 107: <t holds result>
Conclusion
If a<b fails at line 100, control jumps straight to 106, and c>d is never evaluated at all -- this is the short-circuit 
property of AND made explicit. Only when a<b succeeds does control fall through to test c>d as well, and only if 
both succeed does t get set to 1.

Q11. Use SDT rules to translate arithmetic expressions: postfix SDT, apply to a+b*c, 
extend to prefix, annotate a+b*c-d, evaluate its postfix with a stack. (13)
Introduction
This question checks understanding of how the SAME grammar produces different output notations depending 
purely on WHERE the print action is placed in each production -- the underlying parse and tree structure never 
change.
Step 1 — Postfix SDT (print after both operands)
Using the rule E->E1 op E2 {E.code = E1.code||E2.code||op}, applying this to a+b*c gives output a b c * +

Q13. Examine backpatching in intermediate code generation; illustrate if-else 
translation with true/false lists and forward-jump resolution. (13)
Introduction
This question asks specifically about the mechanism of backpatching itself -- the three functions that make it 
work -- rather than just a single worked example, so the answer should explain the machinery before applying it.
Step 1 — Explain the Three Backpatch Functions
• makelist(i): returns a new list containing only quad i (one incomplete jump).
• merge(p1,p2): concatenates two lists into a single combined list.
• backpatch(p,i): fills in i as the target label of every jump instruction recorded in list p.
Step 2 — Explain Why Forward-Jump Resolution Is Needed
In a single left-to-right pass, a forward jump's real target -- the start of an else-branch, or the statement after a 
whole if-else -- is code that has not been generated yet at the moment the jump itself must be emitted. 
Backpatching defers filling in that target until it actually becomes known, avoiding any need for a second 
compiler pass purely to fix up jumps.
Step 3 — Worked Example: if (a<b) then x=y+z else x=y-z
100: if a<b goto _   truelist={100}     104: goto _  (patched -> 107 once known)
101: goto _          falselist={101}    105: t2:=y-z
  backpatch(truelist,102); backpatch(falselist,105)
102: t1:=y+z   103: x:=t1                106: x:=t2   107: <next>
Conclusion
This example shows all three functions in use together: makelist implicitly creates truelist/falselist as each jump 
is first emitted, merge would combine lists from multiple sub-expressions in more complex conditions, and 
backpatch resolves each list the moment its true target becomes known -- precisely the general-purpose 
machinery reused throughout every control-flow translation in this unit.

lookups with no backtracking, while a malformed string is caught immediately at the exact point the grammar is 
violated, with panic-mode recovery ensuring the parser does not simply halt on the first error.

Q25. Expound the design principles of a predictive translator; FIRST/FOLLOW 
computation; error detection and recovery, with examples. (13)
Introduction
This is a purely theoretical question (no specific expression to translate), asking for the complete design 
principles behind predictive translation, tying together everything used practically in Q3, Q21, and Section 2.13.
Step 1 — State the Grammar Requirement
The grammar must be LL(1)-ready: left recursion eliminated (since a predictive parser would otherwise loop 
forever trying to expand a left-recursive non-terminal), and common prefixes left-factored (since the parser 
must choose a production using only one token of lookahead, with no backtracking to try an alternative later).
Step 2 — State the FIRST and FOLLOW Rules
FIRST rules: a terminal maps to itself; an eps-production adds eps; X->Y1Y2... adds FIRST(Y1), and continues 
adding FIRST(Yi) for later Yi only while every earlier Yj can derive eps. FOLLOW rules: $ is in FOLLOW(start 
symbol); A->aBb adds FIRST(b)-{eps} to FOLLOW(B); A->aB, or eps in FIRST(b), adds all of FOLLOW(A) to 
FOLLOW(B).
Step 3 — Explain Table Construction and Error Handling
Table build: A->alpha goes in M[A,a] for every a in FIRST(alpha), and additionally in M[A,b] for every b in 
FOLLOW(A) whenever eps is in FIRST(alpha); if any cell ends up with two or more entries, the grammar is not 
LL(1) and predictive parsing cannot be used as-is. Error detection: a blank cell for the current (non-terminal, 
token) pair signals an error immediately, at the exact point of the mismatch. Recovery: if the offending token is 
in FOLLOW(A), pop A silently (panic mode) and continue -- exactly as demonstrated for (3+)*5 in Q21.
Conclusion
Together, these principles guarantee that a predictive translator never needs to backtrack, never gets stuck 
without a defined action, and can recover gracefully from malformed input by treating a non-terminal as having 
matched empty input whenever doing so is grammatically safe (i.e. the next token is something that non-
terminal's parent could legally see afterward anyway).

Introduction
This is a five-part question that walks the same underlying expression through every representation covered in 
this unit -- from postfix decoding all the way to final three-address code -- so each of the five parts should be 
treated as its own mini-derivation rather than a one-line answer.
(i) Dependency Graph
Decoding the postfix string ab+c*de-/ with a stack first reconstructs the tree corresponding to ((a+b)*c)/(d-e). 
Naming its internal nodes N1=a+b, N2=N1*c, N3=d-e, N4(root)=N2/N3, the dependency graph records exactly 
which attribute values feed into which others:
a -> N1   b -> N1   N1 -> N2   c -> N2   d -> N3   e -> N3   N2 -> N4   N3 -> N4
(ii) Order of Attribute Evaluation (Topological Sort)
1. a.val, b.val (leaves) -> 2. N1.val = a.val+b.val
3. c.val (leaf) -> 4. N2.val = N1.val*c.val
5. d.val, e.val (leaves) -> 6. N3.val = d.val-e.val
7. N4.val (root) = N2.val / N3.val
This order is valid because every edge in the dependency graph above points strictly from an earlier-evaluated 
node to a later one -- no node is ever needed before it has itself been computed.
(iii) Infix and Prefix Forms
Reading the same tree in-order gives the infix form ((a+b)*c)/(d-e); reading it pre-order gives the prefix form / * 
+ a b c - d e. Both are simply different traversal orders of the identical tree the postfix string decoded into.
(iv) Annotated Parse Tree
        N4.val = N2.val/N3.val
       /                       \
  N2.val=N1.val*c.val      N3.val=d.val-e.val
   /            \             /         \
 N1.val=a+b     c.val       d.val       e.val
(v) Three-Address Code
t1 := a + b     t2 := t1 * c     t3 := d - e     t4 := t2 / t3
Conclusion
Every one of these five views -- the dependency graph, the evaluation order, the two alternate notations, the 
annotated tree, and the TAC -- describes exactly the same underlying computation. The only thing that changes 
across them is which piece of information (structure, order, notation, computed value, or final instructions) is 
being made explicit.

Introduction
This question specifically includes the extra start symbol L->E (a common Anna University grammar convention 
for wrapping the whole expression), so part of a full answer is explaining WHY the grammar nests the way it 
does, not only computing the final number.
(i)-(ii) Parse Tree, Annotated with Values
F->(E) parses each parenthesised group as an E nested inside an F. T->T*F combines the two parenthesised 
values via multiplication. E->T and L->E simply pass the value up unchanged to the root -- these two productions 
exist purely to connect the expression grammar to the start symbol, contributing no computation of their own.
L.val = 77
 |
E.val = 77  (root, via E->T)
        /                    \
  E1.val=3+4=7          T.val=5+6=11
   (via T->F->(E))        (via F->(E))
    |                          |
  T:3+4                    E2:5+6
(iii) Dependency Graph
DIGIT(3).val and DIGIT(4).val feed into E1.val (the first parenthesised group); DIGIT(5).val and DIGIT(6).val feed 
into E2.val (the second group). Then E1.val -> F1.val -> T.val, E2.val -> F2.val -> T.val, and finally T.val -> E.val -> 
L.val, chaining all the way to the root.
(iv)-(v) Bottom-Up Evaluation Sequence and Final Value
Step Node Rule Value
1 E1 (=3+4) E1.val = 3+4 7
2 F1 (=(E1)) F1.val = E1.val 7
3 E2 (=5+6) E2.val = 5+6 11
4 F2 (=(E2)) F2.val = E2.val 11
5 T (=F1*F2) T.val = F1.val * F2.val 77
6 E, L (root) E.val = T.val; L.val = E.val 77 (final)
Conclusion
The two parenthesised groups (3+4) and (5+6) are entirely independent of each other and could be evaluated in 
either order, or even simultaneously -- only the final multiplication at T genuinely needs both to be finished, 
giving the confirmed final value 77.

Introduction
This question requires composing two ideas covered separately elsewhere in this unit: short-circuit evaluation of 
a boolean 'and', and backpatching for an if-then-else -- so the answer should make clear how the two 
mechanisms connect rather than treating them as separate problems.
(i)-(ii) Expression Tree and Short-Circuit Representation
         if-then-else
      /       |        \
   AND     x=y+z      x=y-z
  /   \
a<b   c>d
Let E1=(a<b), E2=(c>d). For E1 and E2, the short-circuit rule states: backpatch(E1.truelist, start-of-E2's code); 
E.truelist = E2.truelist; E.falselist = merge(E1.falselist, E2.falselist). In plain terms: c>d is only ever evaluated once 
a<b has already been confirmed true.
(iii) and (v) Final Labelled TAC
100: if a<b goto 102     105: x:=t1
101: goto 107            106: goto 109
102: if c>d goto 104     107: t2:=y-z
103: goto 107            108: x:=t2
104: t1:=y+z             109: <next statement>
(iv) Backpatching Steps
E1.truelist={100} is patched to 102 -- this is precisely the short-circuit connection point, since it means 'only test 
c>d if a<b already succeeded.' E2.truelist={102} is patched to 104, the then-branch, since reaching there means 
BOTH conditions held. merge(E1.falselist={101}, E2.falselist={103}) is patched to 107, the else-branch, since 
either condition alone failing should lead there. Finally, the then-branch's trailing goto (106) is patched last, to 
109, once the else-branch's length is known.
Conclusion
The key insight examiners look for here is that E1.truelist is NOT patched directly to the then-branch (104) -- it is 
patched to the START OF E2's code (102), which is exactly what implements the short-circuit behaviour: passing 
the first test only buys the right to attempt the second one, not immediate entry into the then-branch.

Q5. Discuss the foundational principles of a type system and a simple type checker. 
Examine type expressions, equivalence, and implicit/explicit conversions; 
demonstrate type checking for a mixed expression. (15)
Introduction
This is the most theory-heavy Part C question, requiring a structured discussion across four distinct sub-topics 
before a worked example ties them together.
Foundational Principles
A type system assigns a type to every expression and enforces that each operator receives operands of a 
permitted type. A type checker is the specific translator that computes types bottom-up over the syntax tree 
and reports type_error wherever a rule is violated; critically, type_error propagates upward as the type of its 
containing expression, so a single mismatch does not cause a cascade of further spurious errors as the checker 
continues up the tree.
Type Expressions
Basic types: integer, float/real, char, boolean, void, and the special type_error. Constructors build compound 
types from these: array(n,T) for arrays, T1xT2 for products/records, pointer(T) for pointers, and T1->T2 for 
functions.

Implicit conversion (coercion) is inserted automatically by the compiler -- e.g. widening an int to float. Explicit 
conversion (casting) is written directly by the programmer -- e.g. (int) x -- and may narrow a value, losing

b*c: (int,float) -> widen b -> float.   a+(b*c): (int,float) -> widen a -> float.

Conclusion
These four ideas form a single coherent pipeline in a real compiler: type expressions give the notation, 
equivalence rules decide when two type expressions match, the type-checking rule table decides what happens 
when they don't quite match but are still compatible, and conversions (implicit or explicit) are the concrete code 
inserted as a result.

(iv) Role of Type Checking
Type checking runs alongside code generation, not as a separate later pass: before each instruction above is 
emitted, the checker verifies that its operands' types are compatible and inserts any needed conversion (such as 
inttoreal) exactly at that point, or flags type_error if no valid rule applies.
(v) Advantages of Intermediate Code
• Machine independence: only the code generator needs to change to retarget the compiler to a new 
machine.
• Reusable optimisation: machine-independent optimisations can be written once against the uniform TAC 
form and applied for every target.
• Simplicity: TAC is far easier to analyse and transform than either raw source text or final machine code.
• Modularity: front-end and back-end phases can be developed, tested, and reused independently of each 
other.
Conclusion
This example shows type checking and TAC generation as two aspects of the same single traversal of the syntax 
tree, while the advantages listed explain WHY compilers bother with this intermediate step at all rather than 
translating source code directly into machine instructions.
Q7. Design a syntax-directed translator for arithmetic expressions: SDD/SDT rules 
for attribute evaluation, bottom-up evaluation, intermediate code for (a+b)*(c-d)+e, 
and backpatching's role in control-flow translation. (15)
Introduction
This final Part C question is the most integrative in the bank, requiring the SDD/SDT distinction, a concrete 
worked translation, AND an explanation of how backpatching extends the same ideas to control-flow statements 
-- effectively a summary question covering the whole unit.
SDD vs SDT
An SDD states WHAT each attribute's value is, without committing to an evaluation order -- it is a specification. A 
Translation Scheme (SDT) embeds semantic actions directly within the production body, fixing WHEN each 
action fires relative to parsing -- it is an implementation, and is what actually drives code emission during a 
single parsing pass.
SDT Rules for This Translator
E -> E1+E2 {E.place=newtemp(); emit(E.place ':=' E1.place '+' E2.place)}
E -> E1-E2 {...similarly with '-'}
E -> E1*E2 {...similarly with '*'}
E -> (E1)  {E.place = E1.place}

t1 := a + b    t2 := c - d    t3 := t1 * t2    t4 := t3 + e
Every E.place above is synthesized purely from children, so the entire translation is produced in one bottom-up 
pass: t1(=a+b) and t2(=c-d) are computed first (in either order, since they are independent), then t3=t1*t2, and 
finally t4=t3+e.
Role of Backpatching in Control-Flow Translation
Control-flow statements differ fundamentally from plain arithmetic expressions: a jump's target -- an else-
branch, a loop exit -- is code that has not yet been generated when the jump itself must be emitted, in a single 
left-to-right pass. Backpatching resolves this by recording every such incomplete jump in a truelist, falselist, or 
nextlist, and filling in the real address only once it becomes known -- exactly the mechanism used throughout 
Part 5 and Part 3 to translate if-then-else and while statements correctly in one pass.
Conclusion
This question demonstrates that SDT and backpatching are not two separate techniques but one continuous 
idea applied at different levels: SDT fixes the order in which simple synthesized attributes (like E.place) are 
computed for expressions, while backpatching extends that same single-pass philosophy to control-flow 
constructs, where the 'attribute' being resolved is a jump target rather than a numeric value.
